scribe_response.text: Tell me about something you are proud of. The thing I um am proudest of is, of is the garden we built at Saint Aldric's in nineteen ninety-four. I was in charge uh of the older people's part, up on the, the second, the second floor. The people there looked at a wall all day, and I hated that. Down below uh was a little place full of old rusty things and weeds. One morning I looked um down, down from the um window and decided it should be a garden. I wrote to the uh people in charge, and uh they said no, politely. I wrote another, and the board sent me a note about budgets um and insurance. So I stopped writing letters uh and started digging instead, early on Sunday mornings. My husband came with a spade, and he said I was mad, but he came. We did the weeds first, weeds first, and they stung me right through my gloves. A man took the rusty things away on a t- trolley and asked nothing. Another man found us some old stones from a building that had come down. I wrote to lots of places asking uh for anything they uh could spare. One place sent us a load of plants and some soil for nothing. The group I sang with did a sale and, and made enough for a seat. What happened next? We made beds uh that were up high, so nobody had to bend down to touch um things. I put some purple plants along the path, because they smell nice uh and bees like them. The flowers went up a frame um that my husband, husband made from sticks and string. Some of the older staff thought I was mad, and one said it was not work. I told her I thought it was exactly what the work was. The first person to go out was a um woman who had not spoken for ages. Two of them took her down, and she put her hand in the plants. She said it smelled like her mum's cupboard, and then she uh cried, cried quietly. After that the ward changed, and I could feel um it, it, like a window opened in um a stuffy room. I had a patient once who was very kind um to me. He was good with um his hands, and he uh made me something for my birthday. It was a little bird, little bird, and he gave it to me with a smile. I look at it every morning when I um make my tea. It always reminds me of him. Men who had refused to get out of bed asked um for a cushion and a cardigan. Can you tell me more about that? We had a tea um party in the um summer, with um c- cakes and uh some men with instruments. Even the important man came, and he ate lots and said I was right. The people in charge came to look, and I stood there feeling very nervous. The chairman looked at the patients laughing in the sun and took off, off his hat. He said maybe that wall should have been a garden all along. They gave us a uh small budget the next, next year, and I spent every penny on bulbs. Spring after spring the daffodils came up, and the uh patients held them like small trumpets. When I stopped working, the staff put, put my name on a seat. It had um a little plate, and I felt too shy um to read it out. I have never been much good at speeches, and I was not asked, not asked to make one. Instead, the nurses sang for me, uh rather b- badly, and I loved every note. I am proud of what they make, but that garden was mine. It showed me that a stubborn woman with a spade can change a whole ward. I have heard that it is still there, though the old wing has um been uh rebuilt around it. When I smell those purple flowers, I think of that place and that woman's hand.
